statusDefinitions.schematic: Illustrative proportions; not a measured survey.

schema.note: The current collection is a schematic proportional study, not a measured survey or a claim about every church.

studies.name: Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Ravenna nomination
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO describes the basilica as 56 m long by 30 m wide; the Atlas drawing dimensions, module, radius, and height are schematic readings, not a measured survey.
studies.surfaceNote: The nave is read as a repeated bay module: length is a sequence, while the apse closes the axis with a single primary radius.
studies.exteriorNote: A long rectangular envelope is extended by a half-circle apse; the side aisles keep the main axis legible from the outside.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, paired column lines turn the rectangle into a measured procession of bays, with the apse as the final radial room.

studies.name: Notre-Dame de Chartres Cathedral
studies.source: Cathédrale de Chartres · official architecture guide
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the cathedral's official guide reports 130.20 m overall length, a 37.50 m vault height, and a 16.40 m nave span; Atlas envelope values remain a schematic comparison model.
studies.surfaceNote: The pointed arch converts a regular bay into a vertical instrument: repeated modules rise toward a high, narrow crown.
studies.exteriorNote: A cruciform plan, flying-buttress rhythm, and faceted apse create a directional envelope with a strong vertical bias.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, pointed ribs resolve each bay into a self-similar frame; the eye follows the axis upward as much as forward.

studies.name: Hosios Loukas Katholikon
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Hosios Loukas Monastery
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO describes the Katholikon as an 11th-century cross-in-square church with a central dome; Atlas envelope and module values are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: Four equal arms lock into a square field, turning the central dome into the geometric and visual center of the room.
studies.exteriorNote: The exterior gathers around a compact square and a dominant central drum; secondary volumes register the cross beneath it.
studies.interiorNote: The inner geometry is a sequence of nested squares and arcs: a centered room where radial balance matters more than procession.

studies.name: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
studies.source: Chiesa di Sant'Andrea al Quirinale · official architecture guide
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the Jesuit church was designed by Bernini and built from 1658 to 1678; the official guide identifies its elliptical plan. Atlas envelope dimensions are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: An ellipse replaces the static circle: its two radii pull the room between centered gathering and directional movement.
studies.exteriorNote: The outer wall reads as a sequence of convex and concave curves, held by a rectangular frontage and a shallow transept.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the oval is a controlled distortion of the circle—compressing the sides while extending the ceremonial axis.

studies.name: Borgund Stave Church
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the managing heritage foundation dates the church to about 1180; the Atlas uses its post-and-frame geometry as a schematic proportional reading.
studies.surfaceNote: A small footprint becomes tall through stacked frames: the module is narrow, repeated, and pulled upward into the roof.
studies.exteriorNote: Nested rooflines create a stepped silhouette; the envelope is compact in plan but layered in section.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, a forest of posts makes the structural module visible, turning vertical repetition into the room’s ornament.

studies.name: Church of the Light
studies.churchName: Ibaraki Kasugaoka Church (Church of the Light)
studies.source: The Museum of Modern Art · Tadao Ando catalogue
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: MoMA describes a rectangular concrete volume completed in 1987–89; the Atlas uses a normalized schematic envelope to study its axial light cut, not a measured survey.
studies.surfaceNote: The primary figure is a precise frame interrupted by light: a clear module with one deliberate asymmetry to admit the sky.
studies.exteriorNote: A folded, off-axis envelope makes the wall and roof read as one continuous geometric gesture.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the room is reduced to a few planes and a measured opening; the section becomes the main ornament.

studies.name: Basilica of San Vitale
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO identifies San Vitale as one of Ravenna's 5th–6th-century Early Christian Monuments and a major Byzantine work; Atlas dimensions and modules are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The octagonal field distributes attention around a luminous center, turning enclosure into a sequence of equal thresholds.
studies.exteriorNote: A compact polygonal shell gathers smaller volumes around a dominant central drum and dome.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the ring of piers makes the center feel both contained and continuously approached from every direction.

studies.name: Hagia Sophia
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Historic Areas of Istanbul
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO identifies Hagia Sophia as a 6th-century Byzantine masterpiece designed in 532–537; Atlas dimensions and dome proportions are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: A broad central field is lifted by a single dome, making the transition from square support to circular crown the primary event.
studies.exteriorNote: The outer silhouette layers buttresses, half-domes, and a central crown into a stepped geometric mass.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, pendentive-like transitions turn a rectilinear room into a suspended radial field of light.

studies.name: Speyer Cathedral
studies.churchName: Imperial Cathedral Basilica of the Assumption and St Stephen
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Speyer Cathedral
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO describes Speyer Cathedral as a Romanesque basilica founded in 1030 and remodelled at the end of the 11th century; Atlas dimensions are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The Romanesque field is read as a measured procession of heavy bays, interrupted by the crossing and resolved by paired towers.
studies.exteriorNote: A long basilican envelope is thickened by towers, transept arms, and a sequence of rounded volumes.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, repeated bays carry the eye toward the crossing while the vault registers weight through rhythm rather than height.

studies.name: Durham Cathedral
studies.churchName: Cathedral Church of Christ, Blessed Mary the Virgin and St Cuthbert
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the cathedral's official guide describes its Romanesque design and historic quire; Atlas dimensions, modules, and vault profile are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The nave becomes a sequence of thick structural frames, so the longitudinal axis is carried by repetition and vault ribs.
studies.exteriorNote: A compact Romanesque mass rises from strong piers and towers, with the roofline acting as a stepped counterpoint to the ground plan.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, alternating supports and ribbed vaults turn weight into a visible cadence along the nave.

studies.name: Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela
studies.churchName: Cathedral Basilica of Santiago de Compostela
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the cathedral's official history dates the Romanesque construction from 1075 and its consecration to 1211; Atlas dimensions and procession are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The pilgrimage church is read as a long sequence that repeatedly widens, pauses, and turns before returning to the central axis.
studies.exteriorNote: A compact basilican body is gathered by transept arms and a dense ring of chapels around the eastern end.
studies.interiorNote: The plan choreographs movement through nave, transept, and ambulatory, making the axis legible as a ritual route.

studies.name: Notre-Dame de Reims Cathedral
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Reims Cathedral
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO describes Reims Cathedral as a masterpiece of 13th-century Gothic art whose sculpture is integral to its architecture; Atlas dimensions are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The geometry is a vertical instrument: bays repeat horizontally while sculpture and pointed arches pull the eye upward.
studies.exteriorNote: A cruciform plan is thickened by buttresses, towers, and a layered sculptural façade that keeps the axis visible from afar.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the elevation is organized as a calibrated stack of arcade, triforium, and clerestory.

studies.name: Cologne Cathedral
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Cologne Cathedral
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO records construction beginning in 1248 and completion in 1880, with later builders following the medieval design; Atlas dimensions remain schematic.
studies.surfaceNote: The cathedral is read as an almost continuous vertical grid, where the persistence of one design keeps centuries aligned.
studies.exteriorNote: A dense Gothic silhouette concentrates towers, buttresses, and tracery around a strict longitudinal field.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the five-aisled section multiplies the vertical rhythm while preserving a strong central procession.

studies.name: Monreale Cathedral
studies.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre · Arab-Norman Palermo and Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: UNESCO includes Monreale Cathedral in the Arab-Norman Palermo and Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale World Heritage property; Atlas dimensions and ornament geometry are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The basilican axis is overlaid with a dense field of repeated pattern, making surface and procession inseparable.
studies.exteriorNote: A restrained outer shell conceals a layered interior order of arches, columns, and luminous surfaces.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the nave becomes a measured sequence of bays whose repeated surfaces turn geometry into iconographic atmosphere.

studies.name: Basilica Cathedral of Saint-Denis

studies.exteriorNote: The façade and towers establish a directional frame, while the eastern end gathers around a radiating ambulatory.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, pointed arches and stained-glass openings turn the perimeter into a luminous geometric membrane.

studies.name: Urnes Stave Church

studies.exteriorNote: Layered roofs and carved edges make the timber shell appear to grow upward from a compact footprint.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, posts and braces keep the structural grid close to the body, turning enclosure into a tactile rhythm.

studies.exteriorNote: The timber envelope expands and contracts through stacked volumes, building a skyline from repeated geometric peaks.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the frame concentrates upward movement around a central vertical field and a dense sequence of supports.

studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: Venice's official city guide identifies the church as a complex Palladian project; Atlas dimensions and proportional readings are schematic.

studies.exteriorNote: The façade layers temple-like fronts over the church body, making proportion legible as a public image.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, paired columns and crossing volumes establish a measured field in which symmetry guides movement.

studies.exteriorNote: A layered front and domed body create a clear ceremonial silhouette across the lagoon.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, column screens and shallow chapels produce a measured rhythm that alternates between enclosure and openness.

studies.name: St Paul's Cathedral
studies.source: City of London · Protected Views SPD / St Paul's dimensions
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the City of London survey table reports 169.2 m length, 75.0 m greatest breadth, and 111.6 m height; those three envelope fields are published-reference dimensions, while the Atlas radius, module, bay count, and geometric reading remain schematic.
studies.surfaceNote: A long ceremonial axis is interrupted and intensified by the dome, turning the crossing into a spatial hinge.
studies.exteriorNote: The outer shell pairs a classical order with a dominant dome, giving the city a stable centered silhouette.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, longitudinal movement and circular gathering are held in tension by the crossing and its layered heights.

studies.name: Karlskirche
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the official Karlskirche history records the foundation stone in 1716 and describes its layered Baroque and cross-cultural forms; Atlas dimensions are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: The building is read as a stack of cultural geometries—portico, triumphal towers, and dome—held in one broad composition.
studies.exteriorNote: A wide front gathers columns, towers, and a high dome into a layered pyramid of symbolic forms.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the dome becomes an upward field of light while the longitudinal order keeps the room ceremonial.

studies.name: Chapelle Notre-Dame-du-Haut

studies.surfaceNote: The chapel is read as a thick curved boundary whose asymmetry gathers light, weight, and orientation into one gesture.
studies.exteriorNote: A heavy roof and irregular shell create a low, sculptural silhouette that turns toward the landscape.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, small openings and curved walls make light feel like a set of calibrated cuts through mass.

studies.source: Catedral Metropolitana de Brasília · official history
studies.sourceNote: Real reference building: the cathedral's official history attributes its modern symbolic design to Oscar Niemeyer and records its 16 parabolic concrete columns; Atlas dimensions are schematic readings.
studies.surfaceNote: Sixteen repeated structural gestures turn the circular plan into a crown, with the center held open for light and movement.
studies.exteriorNote: The concrete ribs rise and lean inward, producing a singular crown-like envelope around the lower glazed volume.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, the radial structure and suspended figures make the room feel continuous rather than divided into bays.

studies.name: Thorncrown Chapel
studies.source: Thorncrown Chapel · official history and architecture

studies.surfaceNote: A narrow repeated frame turns the woodland setting into part of the room, with the module acting as both structure and view.
studies.exteriorNote: The chapel's transparent timber lattice keeps the envelope light, rhythmic, and visually continuous with the trees.
studies.interiorNote: Inside, repeated triangular frames pull the eye along the axis while the forest remains present through the glass.
